name: Quill
workload: Caller-thread latency of LOG_INFO with int, int, double arguments, 1 thread and 4 threads, nanoseconds per call at several percentiles.
claimed_speedup: 1 thread: Quill unbounded queue 50th/99.9th 6/10 ns vs spdlog 271/360 ns (also vs g3log 1066/1143 and Boost.Log 3093/3621); Quill macro-free mode 11/18 ns.
hardware: Intel Core i5-12600 @ 4.8 GHz, RHEL 9.4, isolated cores, tuned for benchmarking
tradeoffs: Deferred formatting on a backend thread; log arguments are copied into a per-thread queue; C++17; bounded dropping queue can lose messages when full.
caveats: Benchmark is first-party (author of Quill) though the code is public in odygrd/logger_benchmarks; measures caller-side latency only, not end-to-end throughput to disk; system tuned (isolcpus, mitigations off). Last-commit date from github.com commits page.
found_via: GitHub: WebSearch 'C++ asynchronous binary logger nanosecond latency faster than spdlog fmtlog quill'; github.com/topics/logging?l=c%2B%2B

name: fmtlog
workload: Caller-thread latency per log call for six message types (static string, string concat, integers, double, complex format) using spdlog default header pattern, with throughput also reported.
claimed_speedup: README: staticString 6.4 ns vs spdlog 156.4 ns; stringConcat 6.4 vs 209.4; singleInteger 6.3 vs 202.3; twoIntegers 6.4 vs 257.2; complexFormat 6.4 vs 390.9 ns. Independent run in quill README (1 thread, int,int,double): fmtlog 6 ns vs spdlog 271 ns at 50th percentile.
compiler_and_flags: GCC 14.2, Release, -march=x86-64-v3 (per quill README); own README says GCC 10.2 tested
hardware: Intel Core i5-12600 @ 4.8 GHz, RHEL 9.4, isolated cores, tuned for benchmarking; own README run on Intel Xeon Gold 6144 @ 3.50GHz
tradeoffs: Requires fmtlib and C++17; user must call fmtlog::poll() to drain queues; default drops messages when the 1 MB per-thread queue is full (FMTLOG_BLOCK=1 blocks instead); Linux/GCC tested.
caveats: Own README table at https://github.com/MengRao/fmtlog (compiler flags not stated there); tier A relies on quill's third-party-style harness table. Latency only, the throughput column favours binary NanoLog.
found_via: GitHub: WebSearch 'C++ asynchronous binary logger nanosecond latency faster than spdlog fmtlog quill'

name: NanoLog (PlatformLab)
workload: Caller-side runtime latency (50th / 99.9th percentile, ns) for six message types and maximum throughput with 1-16 threads; binary log file with separate decompressor.
claimed_speedup: README: staticString 7/37 ns vs spdlog 214/2546 ns; complexFormat 8/40 vs 1776/5267; also vs glog 1198/5968 and Log4j2, Boost. Over 80 million logs/second. Independent: quill README 1 thread NanoLog 8 ns vs spdlog 271 ns (50th).
hardware: Intel Core i5-12600 @ 4.8 GHz, RHEL 9.4, isolated cores, tuned for benchmarking
tradeoffs: Output is binary and needs the decompressor to read; preprocessor version needs a Python step in the build; C++17 version is closer to a library; POSIX AIO dependency; compiled library is application-specific.
caveats: README compares against spdlog v1.1.0 and glog v0.3.5 (old versions) and does not state compiler flags or CPU in the table page; tier A comes from quill's current-version harness. Last commit 2020 (>3 years).
found_via: GitHub: WebSearch 'github C++ low latency logging library benchmark vs spdlog nanoseconds per log call'

name: NanoLog (Iyengar111)
workload: Caller latency percentiles in microseconds for guaranteed and non-guaranteed loggers, 1-4 threads, vs spdlog, g3log and reckless.
claimed_speedup: 1 thread: spdlog average 2.588590 us, 50th 3 us; NanoLog guaranteed average 0.347930 us (README). Independent: quill README 1 thread NanoLog 106 ns vs spdlog 271 ns (50th).
tradeoffs: Header plus source, standard C++11 only; no license file found, so code cannot be assumed copyable.
caveats: No LICENSE file (raw LICENSE, LICENSE.md, LICENSE.txt, UNLICENSE all 404, GitHub page shows none); compiler flags absent in README; very old toolchain; tier A relies on own public bench file nano_vs_spdlog_vs_g3log_vs_reckless.cpp plus quill harness. Unrelated to PlatformLab NanoLog.
found_via: GitHub: WebSearch 'github header-only C++ logger faster than spdlog benchmark'

name: XTR
workload: Caller-thread latency of formatted log calls in quill's logger_benchmarks harness (1 and 4 threads, int,int,double).
claimed_speedup: Quill README: XTR 1 thread 50th/99.9th 6/10 ns vs spdlog 271/360 ns; 4 threads XTR 8 ns at 50th. Own README shows 0.894 ns to 8.83 ns per call on Ryzen 5950X but with no baseline comparison.
hardware: Intel Core i5-12600 @ 4.8 GHz, RHEL 9.4, isolated cores, tuned for benchmarking
tradeoffs: Linux and FreeBSD x86-64 only; no allocations or syscalls on the log path; background consumer thread; custom I/O backends.
caveats: Own README benchmark (Ryzen 5950X, g++ 15.3.0) does not compare with spdlog; the spdlog comparison exists only in quill's README by quill's author.
found_via: GitHub: quill README latency table, discovered via search 'C++ asynchronous binary logger nanosecond latency faster than spdlog fmtlog quill'

name: binlog (Morgan Stanley)
workload: Caller-thread latency of structured binary logging (1 thread, int,int,double) in quill's harness.
claimed_speedup: Quill README 1 thread: MS BinLog 50th/99.9th 18/119 ns vs spdlog 271/360 ns.
hardware: Intel Core i5-12600 @ 4.8 GHz, RHEL 9.4, isolated cores, tuned for benchmarking
tradeoffs: Structured binary log files need a bread/binlog tool to read; header-heavy C++17.
caveats: Repo archived 2026-07-01 (read-only), so maintenance is abandoned; the numbers come only from quill's README; own README makes a qualitative claim only.

name: BqLog
workload: 1-10 threads each writing 2,000,000 log entries with 4 parameters; total time until all logs are flushed to disk, spdlog async file logger with blocking policy, glog sync.
claimed_speedup: README: compressed mode 6-65x faster than spdlog (async), 47-252x faster than glog, 7-16x faster than fmtlog, 7-18x faster than quill (1 thread: BqLog Compress 95 ms vs spdlog 560 ms vs fmtlog 672 ms vs quill 639 ms, text mode 258 ms). Quill README: BqLog 125 ns vs spdlog 271 ns caller latency (50th).
stars_or_usage: 645 stars; used in Honor of Kings
tradeoffs: Binary compressed appender needs a decoder tool; multi-language wrappers (Java, C#, Python, Go, TypeScript); heavier library than header-only loggers.
caveats: First-party benchmark on Windows/MSVC only, with the author's own benchmark code; fmtlog and quill baselines are older versions (quill 11.1.0); by quill's latency measure BqLog is slower than fmtlog and quill, so the win is throughput to disk. Benchmark README also notes glog has no async mode.

name: slick-logger
workload: Operations per second for small messages (literal only) and medium messages (int, double, string), 1-8 threads, vs spdlog 1.12.0 async and sync.
claimed_speedup: Small messages 1 thread 7,669,915 ops/s vs spdlog_async 3,765,386 and spdlog_sync 1,298,350; 8 threads 10,960,620 vs 1,925,261 and 490,994. Medium 1 thread 4,750,287 vs 899,182 and 575,968.
hardware: AMD Ryzen 9 5900HX, 32 GB, Windows 11 Pro, local NVMe
tradeoffs: C++20 with std::format; header-only plus slick-queue dependency; lock-free MPMC ring, deferred formatting on writer thread, shared-memory multi-process mode.
caveats: First-party Windows/MSVC benchmark; measures producer-side ops/s, not time to durable disk; spdlog 1.12.0 is not the latest; author warns numbers describe one machine.
found_via: GitHub: WebSearch 'github C logging library lock-free ring buffer glog faster benchmark'

name: lockfreelog
workload: Sustained messages per second logging to a file from a single producer vs spdlog async, fmt, printf and iostream.
claimed_speedup: ~28M msgs/sec vs spdlog async ~5M (5.3x) and printf ~12M (2.3x) on Apple M3; ~50M msgs/sec on Xeon Gold 6348 (README).
hardware: Apple M3 (macOS) and Intel Xeon Gold 6348 (Linux)
tradeoffs: Header-only C++20, single lock-free ring slot publish, consumer spins/yields when idle (CPU cost), fixed slot message size.
caveats: No license stated, so reference only; brand new repo with 3 commits; spdlog version not stated on the page; first-party; benchmark code in bench/benchmark.cpp not opened.
found_via: GitHub: WebSearch 'github C logging library lock-free ring buffer glog faster benchmark'

name: Serenity Logger
workload: Single-threaded, 400-byte C-string message, 1,000,000 iterations, console (output disabled), file and rotating-file targets.
claimed_speedup: README: file target 215.981 ns vs spdlog basic file sink 1125.735 ns; rotating 627.968 vs 2919.572 ns; console 5.656 vs 10.837 ns (README says ~40-42%, ~79-81%, ~78-79% faster).
tradeoffs: C++20; built-in formatter or std::format (MSVC) or fmtlib; alpha, README calls it a learning project.
caveats: Numbers dated 05Jul22; compiler, flags and CPU not stated; single thread only; author calls the test 'very crude'; console figures disabled output; spdlog version not stated. Last commit date not confirmed.
